text: This is a walkthrough of SignalCore, an evidence engine for product operations. Over the next ten minutes, you'll see how it turns customer noise into a prioritized backlog, using a live run of the working prototype.

SignalCore answers one question for a product team: what should we build next, and why? It reads three independent sources of truth. What customers say, from Gong calls, support tickets, the idea portal and advisory board notes. What they do, from product telemetry. And what they pay, from the CRM. The demo tenant is a fictional identity and device management company, with fourteen hundred customer voices, three hundred and thirty-six thousand product events, and five hundred and seventy deals. The data is synthetic, but every number you'll see was produced by the pipeline, not typed in by hand.

Let's start with the engine. This is the run view. I'll replay the recorded live run, so every model response is the one Claude actually produced. The pipeline is a LangGraph state machine. First, an identity resolver matches messy reporter emails and company names to accounts. The CAB Agent, running on Claude Sonnet, reads six advisory board meeting notes and extracts seventy-nine customer statements, with their line numbers. Claude Haiku labels every item for urgency, sentiment and workarounds, in batches. The Cluster Agent groups the product feedback, and Claude Opus names each theme and rejects clusters that aren't coherent. Then plain SQL joins each theme to telemetry and revenue, and a dependency tracer follows Jira links across teams. Code computes the Evidence Score and the Cost of Delay. The Skeptic Agent, on Claude Opus with read-only SQL access, then tries to refute every theme. Finally, the PBR Agent writes product business reviews, and a Grounding Judge checks every claim before anything reaches leadership.

Because the data is synthetic, the ground truth is known, so the pipeline can be graded. The agents never see these labels. All twelve planted themes were found, with ninety-nine percent cluster precision. All five planted patterns were recovered. Advisory board statements were extracted with perfect precision and recall, and the planted bottleneck epic was found. The trace on the left logs every step, with its model, tokens and cost. The whole live run cost about two dollars and ninety cents.

Now the outputs. This is the prioritization view. Each bubble is a theme. Across the bottom is its Evidence Score: how confident we are that the problem is real and material. Up the side is its Cost of Delay: what one more week of waiting costs, in retention risk and in deals that are stuck. The top right is do now. The top left is validate fast: costly if true, but the evidence is weak, so run a cheap test before you build. Bubble size is C D 3, cost of delay divided by duration, and the backlog below is ranked by it.

The number one priority is a surprise. Patch policies stop applying after OS upgrades. Only seven accounts complained, but usage fell forty-one percent across thirty-four accounts that renew in the next five months. That's a silent churn pattern, and support would never have flagged it. The panel shows the full arithmetic. An Evidence Score of fifty-nine, times a cost of delay of about a hundred and ninety-eight thousand dollars a week, gives an adjusted cost of delay of a hundred and seventeen thousand. Divide by four weeks of work, plus four weeks blocked behind another team's notifications epic, and you get the C D 3 that ranks it first. Below are the three pillars, the rule checks, and the Skeptic's verdict. It weakened this theme, because the dollar figure leans on large accounts that never complained. That tension is the point. The score shows its work, so you can argue with it.

Compare that with Globex. A one point two four million dollar prospect wants custom SAML transforms, and the request is already committed on the roadmap. The rule checks find that ninety-eight percent of the money comes from one account, through a single source. The Skeptic Agent ran its own SQL, traced the mentions back to Globex, and cut confidence in half. The evidence score is eight, and it ranks eighteenth of nineteen. This is a commercial mirage. Treat it as a deal-specific scope, not roadmap.

Engineering estimates are inputs, not gospel. Here, a product manager overrides the build estimate for AI agent permission scoping, from ten weeks to six, with a logged reason. SignalCore recalculates C D 3 and the ranking for the whole backlog instantly, without calling a model, and the theme moves up to second place.

The triangulation view plots behavioral friction against revenue. Agent permissions sits at the top right: complaining accounts abandon the policy editor forty-four percent of the time, against eleven percent for everyone else. On the right, the weak evidence detector audits the roadmap as product ops keeps it today. Two commitments fail. The Globex transform engine, and dark mode, which is already in build with fifty-three requesters, but low urgency and no friction.

Portfolio risk detection runs on the same evidence, every run. Fourteen risks, ranked by severity and by the cost of delay at stake, each with a suggested owner. At the top are two dependency bottlenecks. Then the silent churn risk, revenue concentration, weak roadmap bets, and engineering capacity that's running ahead of the evidence.

Here's why the top two risks matter. The dependency tracer follows blocks links in Jira. S S O eighty-eight, a shared policy engine that no team has started, sits upstream of five epics, including agent permissions and device trust. A blocker inherits the confidence adjusted cost of delay of everything downstream. So this unglamorous platform work carries about two hundred and fifty-six thousand dollars a week. The table ranks every epic by the value it releases per week of work.

Advisory board notes are a classic grind. The CAB Agent reads each meeting document and marks pains, asks, praise and vendor commitments, with the exact line each one came from. Pains and asks flow into clustering as customer evidence, and commitments become follow-ups to track.

Crafting product business reviews is the other grind. The PBR Agent drafts a review for the portfolio and for each module, using only a fixed table of computed facts. Every claim cites its facts, and you can open any claim to see them. The Grounding Judge checks numbers in code, and meaning with a second model. In this run, eighty-one percent of claims passed on the first draft. The rest were rewritten, and eight that still failed were dropped, rather than shown to leadership.

The executive view rolls this up for the C-suite: where each module sits in its lifecycle, adoption velocity over twenty-six weeks, and whether engineering capacity follows the cost of delay. AI Agent Access is growing fastest, up nineteen percent, and carries thirty-six percent of the adjusted cost of delay on seven percent of the engineers. Remote Assist and the Admin Console each hold more than a tenth of engineering, against almost none of the demand.

Finally, ask the evidence. It's an agent with two tools: read-only SQL over the CRM, telemetry and scores, and retrieval over every call, ticket and advisory note. Let's ask which roadmap commitments depend on a single account. It finds the Globex commitment, quotes the customer, and recommends treating it as a deal-specific scope. Every number came from a query, and you can open the exact SQL it ran.

Every parameter lives on the method page, so the model can be challenged: the evidence weights, the penalties, the cost of delay assumptions, and how the workflow maps the old grind to the new outputs.

To recap. SignalCore cross-examines what customers say against what they do and pay, prices the cost of waiting, and ranks the backlog by C D 3. The agents are real Claude calls, the scoring is deterministic and auditable, and the results are graded against ground truth. The data is synthetic, so the next step is a ninety-day pilot on your own call, ticket, product analytics and CRM exports. Thanks for watching.
